Previous research indicates that the same knowledge across different languages within LLMs exhibits a degree of shareability. However, most existing MKE methods overlook the connections of the same knowledge between different languages, resulting in knowledge conflicts and limited edit performance. To address this issue, we first investigate how LLMs process multilingual factual knowledge and discover that the same factual knowledge in different languages generally activates a shared set of neurons, which we call language-agnostic factual neurons (LAFNs). These neurons represent the same factual knowledge shared across languages and imply the semantic connections among multilingual knowledge. Inspired by this finding, we propose a new MKE method by Locating and Updating Language-Agnostic Factual Neurons (LU-LAFNs) to edit multilingual knowledge simultaneously, which avoids knowledge conflicts and thus improves edit performance. Experimental results on Bi-ZsRE and MzsRE benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves the best edit performance, indicating the effectiveness and importance of modeling the semantic connections among multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: On the Entity-Level Alignment in Crosslingual Consistency
papers.research_question: What factors give rise to crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and do failures in entity alignment cause inconsistencies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis linking crosslingual consistency to entity-level alignment, introduces two prompting methods (SUBSUB and SUBINJ) that improve factual recall and consistency, and uses mechanistic interpretability to show these methods enhance entity representation alignment through pivot-language processing.
papers.conclusion: Entity alignment is a key factor underlying crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and the proposed prompting methods offer effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction by enhancing this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Crosslingual consistency is strongly correlated with entity alignment across all studied models.
Consistent factual recall rarely occurs without correctly aligning either the subject or object entities between two languages.
The proposed prompting methods SUBSUB and SUBINJ, which incorporate English translations of subjects, substantially improve factual recall accuracy and consistency, especially in English-centric models.
Mechanistic analysis using Logit Lens shows that SUBSUB and SUBINJ interventions reinforce entity representation alignment in the model's internal conceptual space.
The model's conceptual space is biased towards high-resource languages like English, explaining why using English subject translations is more effective than using other languages.
papers.limitation: Inconsistency can also stem from failure in the processing stage – i.e., the model lacks the factual knowledge so it cannot retrieve the correct object in the conceptual space, which is beyond the scope of this paper.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) are expected to recall factual knowledge consistently across languages. However, the factors that give rise to such crosslingual consistency -- and its frequent failure -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we hypothesize that these inconsistencies may arise from failures in entity alignment, the process of mapping subject and object entities into a shared conceptual space across languages. To test this, we assess alignment through entity-level (subject and object) translation tasks, and find that consistency is strongly correlated with alignment across all studied models, with misalignment of subjects or objects frequently resulting in inconsistencies. Building on this insight, we propose SubSub and SubInj, two effective methods that integrate English translations of subjects into prompts across languages, leading to substantial gains in both factual recall accuracy and consistency. Finally, our mechanistic analysis reveals that these interventions reinforce the entity representation alignment in the conceptual space through model's internal pivot-language processing, offering effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction.

papers.title: The Transfer Neurons Hypothesis: An Underlying Mechanism for Language Latent Space Transitions in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: How do multilingual LLMs transfer representations between language-specific latent spaces and a shared semantic latent space, and what neurons are responsible for this transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes and empirically validates the Transfer Neurons Hypothesis, identifying specific MLP neurons that facilitate transitions between language-specific and shared semantic latent spaces in multilingual LLMs, and shows their critical role in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that transfer neurons are a key mechanism for latent space transitions in multilingual LLMs, enabling language-agnostic reasoning and output generation in the input language.
papers.key_findings:
Internal representations in multilingual LLMs form language-specific latent spaces in initial and final layers, converging to a shared semantic latent space in middle layers.
Transfer neurons in the MLP module are responsible for moving representations between language-specific and shared latent spaces.
Type-1 transfer neurons shift inputs to the shared space, while Type-2 neurons shift outputs back to language-specific spaces.
Type-2 neurons exhibit language specificity and are similar to previously identified language-specific neurons.
Deactivating transfer neurons impairs representation alignment and reduces performance on multilingual QA tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have suggested a processing framework for multilingual inputs in decoder-based LLMs: early layers convert inputs into English-centric and language-agnostic representations; middle layers perform reasoning within an English-centric latent space; and final layers generate outputs by transforming these representations back into language-specific latent spaces. However, the internal dynamics of such transformation and the underlying mechanism remain underexplored. Towards a deeper understanding of this framework, we propose and empirically validate The Transfer Neurons Hypothesis: certain neurons in the MLP module are responsible for transferring representations between language-specific latent spaces and a shared semantic latent space. Furthermore, we show that one function of language-specific neurons, as identified in recent studies, is to facilitate movement between latent spaces. Finally, we show that transfer neurons are critical for reasoning in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Can Cross-Lingual Transferability of Multilingual Transformers Be Activated Without End-Task Data?
papers.research_question: Whether the cross-lingual transferability of multilingual Transformers can be activated without end-task data.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PLUG IN-X, a method that reassembles monolingual and multilingual Transformers to perform cross-lingual transfer without end-task data, and shows it successfully activates transferability.
papers.conclusion: PLUG IN-X successfully activates the cross-lingual transferability of multilingual Transformers without accessing the in-house end-task data.
papers.key_findings:
PLUG IN-X successfully activates cross-lingual transferability without accessing end-task data.
The method works on both natural language inference and question answering tasks.
The cross-model representation alignment (measured by L2 distance and cosine similarity) is crucial for transferability.
Ablation studies show that the multilingual encoder, connector, and middle-layer plugging are important components.
The transfer gap decreases as cross-model representation alignment improves.
papers.limitation:
Only tested on two common types of end tasks (text classification and question answering).
Only considers the situation that the end-task models are obtained by finetuning public pretrained models, not black-box models.
future_direction: Study the research question on more types of models such as large language models.
Study the cross-lingual transfer of black-box end-task models.
papers.abstract: Pretrained multilingual Transformers have achieved great success in cross-lingual transfer learning. Current methods typically activate the cross-lingual transferability of multilingual Transformers by fine-tuning them on end-task data. However, the methods cannot perform cross-lingual transfer when end-task data are unavailable. In this work, we explore whether the cross-lingual transferability can be activated without end-task data. We propose a cross-lingual transfer method, named PlugIn-X. PlugIn-X disassembles monolingual and multilingual Transformers into sub-modules, and reassembles them to be the multilingual end-task model. After representation adaptation, PlugIn-X finally performs cross-lingual transfer in a plug-and-play style. Experimental results show that PlugIn-X successfully activates the cross-lingual transferability of multilingual Transformers without accessing end-task data. Moreover, we analyze how the cross-model representation alignment affects the cross-lingual transferability.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: Steering into New Embedding Spaces: Analyzing Cross-Lingual Alignment Induced by Model Interventions in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the finding experts intervention on cross-lingual alignment in multilingual language models?
papers.core_contribution: Intervening on language expert neurons in mLLMs projects embeddings into a new space with enhanced cross-lingual alignment, leading to improved performance on cross-lingual retrieval tasks.
papers.conclusion: The finding-experts intervention enhances cross-lingual alignment in mLLMs, improving retrieval performance, and is recommended for aligning representations across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The finding experts intervention shifts the embedding space, reducing distances between languages and increasing cross-lingual alignment.
Post-intervention, cross-lingual retrieval accuracy improves by up to 2x in top-1 accuracy.
Within-language similarity is preserved in the new embedding space, as shown by paraphrase retrieval accuracy.
Intervention on random neurons does not yield similar improvements, indicating the importance of targeting expert neurons.
The intervention is most effective when the model has been trained on both the intervention-target and the languages to be aligned.
papers.limitation:
Lack of access to training data and procedures for the models, limiting deeper analysis.
PolyLM-13b behaves as an outlier in the analyses, possibly due to training differences.
Only one intervention method (finding experts) is studied, leaving other approaches for future work.
future_direction: Explore the effect of intervention on alignment in controlled settings with known training data.
Compare different model intervention methods to understand their impact on representation space.
papers.abstract: Aligned representations across languages is a desired property in multilingual large language models (mLLMs), as alignment can improve performance in cross-lingual tasks. Typically alignment requires fine-tuning a model, which is computationally expensive, and sizable language data, which often may not be available. A data-efficient alternative to fine-tuning is model interventions -- a method for manipulating model activations to steer generation into the desired direction. We analyze the effect of a popular intervention (finding experts) on the alignment of cross-lingual representations in mLLMs. We identify the neurons to manipulate for a given language and introspect the embedding space of mLLMs pre- and post-manipulation. We show that modifying the mLLM's activations changes its embedding space such that cross-lingual alignment is enhanced. Further, we show that the changes to the embedding space translate into improved downstream performance on retrieval tasks, with up to 2x improvements in top-1 accuracy on cross-lingual retrieval.

papers.title: How do languages influence each other? Studying cross-lingual data sharing during LM fine-tuning
papers.research_question: To what extent, and under which conditions, do multilingual language models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the use of Training Data Attribution (TDA) methods, specifically TracIn, to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level in multilingual language models, finding that models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that languages largely influence one another cross-lingually under various conditions, with cross-lingual sharing increasing during fine-tuning and languages playing both reinforcing and complementary roles.
papers.key_findings:
MLMs rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
Training samples from other languages can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.
The model exhibits different cross-lingual behaviour in zero-shot testing compared to when the test language is seen during fine-tuning.
Even with data imbalances, the model largely benefits from cross-lingual sharing.
For parallel datasets, cross-lingual sharing is high, and for non-parallel datasets, it is still observed but to a lesser extent.
papers.limitation:
Computational expense limited the study to 125 test samples.
The method is restricted to relatively easy classification tasks and not generation or sequence labeling tasks.
The analysis focuses on the fine-tuning stage and does not disentangle pre-training effects.
future_direction: Extending influence function methods to sequence tagging tasks for more fine-grained analysis.
Studying the emergence of cross-lingual abilities during pre-training.
Inspiring future work on studying sharing mechanisms within multi-task and multi-modal models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) are jointly trained on data from many different languages such that representation of individual languages can benefit from other languages' data. Impressive performance on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer shows that these models are capable of exploiting data from other languages. Yet, it remains unclear to what extent, and under which conditions, languages rely on each other's data. In this study, we use TracIn (Pruthi et al., 2020), a training data attribution (TDA) method, to retrieve the most influential training samples seen during multilingual fine-tuning for a particular test language. This allows us to analyse cross-lingual sharing mechanisms of MLLMs from a new perspective. While previous work studied cross-lingual sharing at the level of model parameters, we present the first approach to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level. We find that MLLMs rely on data from multiple languages from the early stages of fine-tuning and that this reliance gradually increases as fine-tuning progresses. We further study how different fine-tuning languages influence model performance on a given test language and find that they can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.

papers.title: Converging to a Lingua Franca: Evolution of Linguistic Regions and Semantics Alignment in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally achieve cross-lingual skill transfer through neuron activation patterns and semantic alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual LLMs develop a common semantic latent space ('Lingua Franca') for processing inputs across languages, with alignment improving through training and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide insights into the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling, offering a foundation for improving cross-lingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron activation patterns are similar for inputs in the same language, revealing key linguistic regions that can be identified and deactivated to impair language-specific performance.
Activation patterns are similar for semantically identical sentences in different languages, indicating mapping to a common semantic space ('Lingua Franca').
With training, key linguistic regions become smaller and activation patterns become more language-agnostic.
Semantic alignment strengthens with training and increased model size, enhancing cross-lingual reasoning ability.
Key neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on BLOOM and LLaMA2 models, may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on specific datasets like Bible and XL-Sum, which may not cover all linguistic nuances.
Methodology based on averaged activation patterns and z-scores may not capture all neuron interactions.
Underlying reasons for patterns remain speculative, requiring further research for causal relationships.
future_direction: Examine a broader range of multilingual LLM architectures.
Utilize more diverse datasets, including low-resource languages.
Apply more sophisticated techniques like causal inference methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, particularly in multilingual contexts. While recent studies suggest that LLMs can transfer skills learned in one language to others, the internal mechanisms behind this ability remain unclear. We observed that the neuron activation patterns of LLMs exhibit similarities when processing the same language, revealing the existence and location of key linguistic regions. Additionally, we found that neuron activation patterns are similar when processing sentences with the same semantic meaning in different languages. This indicates that LLMs map semantically identical inputs from different languages into a "Lingua Franca", a common semantic latent space that allows for consistent processing across languages. This semantic alignment becomes more pronounced with training and increased model size, resulting in a more language-agnostic activation pattern. Moreover, we found that key linguistic neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers of LLMs, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses. Experiments on BLOOM and LLaMA2 support these findings, highlighting the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling up. This paper provides insights into the internal workings of LLMs, offering a foundation for future improvements in their cross-lingual capabilities.

papers.title: Neuron Specialization: Leveraging intrinsic task modularity for multilingual machine translation
papers.research_question: How do neurons in multilingual translation models exhibit language-specific modularity, and can this be leveraged to reduce interference and improve translation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that FFN neurons in multilingual models exhibit language-specific modularity, and introduces Neuron Specialization, a method that leverages this to reduce interference and improve translation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that intrinsic modularity in multilingual models can be leveraged to improve translation performance by reducing interference and enhancing transfer, with Neuron Specialization providing consistent gains.
papers.key_findings:
FFN neurons in multilingual translation models activate in a language-specific way, with overlaps indicating linguistic proximity.
The specialization of neurons evolves across layers, becoming more language-agnostic in the encoder and more specific in the decoder.
The proposed Neuron Specialization method, which updates task-specific neurons via sparse networks, consistently improves translation quality over baselines.
This method effectively reduces negative interference in high-resource languages and boosts knowledge transfer in low-resource languages.
Neuron Specialization is efficient, requiring minimal extra parameters and time compared to adapter-based methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to multilingual machine translation and does not explore other multilingual NLP tasks.
Analysis is confined to feed-forward network components, excluding other Transformer elements like attention mechanisms.
Neuron identification relies on ReLU activation states; other activation functions like GELU are not considered.
future_direction: Extend the exploration to a broader range of Multilingual Natural Language Processing tasks beyond translation.
Investigate the modularity of other Transformer components such as attention mechanisms or layer normalization.
Explore neuron specialization for FFNs using activation functions other than ReLU, such as GELU.
papers.abstract: Training a unified multilingual model promotes knowledge transfer but inevitably introduces negative interference. Language-specific modeling methods show promise in reducing interference. However, they often rely on heuristics to distribute capacity and struggle to foster cross-lingual transfer via isolated modules. In this paper, we explore intrinsic task modularity within multilingual networks and leverage these observations to circumvent interference under multilingual translation. We show that neurons in the feed-forward layers tend to be activated in a language-specific manner. Meanwhile, these specialized neurons exhibit structural overlaps that reflect language proximity, which progress across layers. Based on these findings, we propose Neuron Specialization, an approach that identifies specialized neurons to modularize feed-forward layers and then continuously updates them through sparse networks. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves consistent performance gains over strong baselines with additional analyses demonstrating reduced interference and increased knowledge transfer.

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs form shared representations across languages with language-specific decoding, and why does performance favor the dominant training language such as English?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs form a shared language-agnostic representation space in middle layers, with language-specific decoding in late layers; performance gaps are mechanistically explained by tokenizer bias and feature strength differences.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs use shared representations in middle layers and language-specific decoding in late layers, with performance gaps explained by feature strength and tokenizer bias.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs consistently form a shared language-agnostic space in middle layers, regardless of English dominance in training data.
Language-specific decoding depends on a small set of high-frequency features in late layers that linearly encode language identity from early layers.
Non-English performance failures are linked to dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias forcing early layers to specialize in word reassembly.
Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding.
The shared multilingual space emerges as an architectural property, even when models are trained without English.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why does performance favor the dominant training language? To address this, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal multilingual shared representations: the model employs highly similar features across languages, while language-specific decoding emerges in later layers. Training models without English shows identical multilingual shared space structures. Decoding relies partly on a small set of high-frequency features in the final layers, which linearly encode language identity from early layers. Intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, to explain non-English failures, we perform a Model-Diffing experiment: underperformance arises from dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias toward English that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their links, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual gaps. Our models and CLTs are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-clts and https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-gpt2-models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/abirharrasse/MultilingualCLTs

papers.title: Beyond Neural Incompatibility: Easing Cross-Scale Knowledge Transfer in Large Language Models through Latent Semantic Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we enable effective and efficient knowledge transfer across LLMs of different scales? The paper investigates using activations as the medium and latent semantic alignment as a prerequisite for parametric knowledge transfer.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a semantics-first method for parametric knowledge transfer that uses layer outputs as the medium and aligns latent semantics between teacher and student models, enabling stable cross-scale transfer.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that treating activations as the carrier of knowledge and aligning semantics-first provides a robust path to cross-scale parametric knowledge transfer, as demonstrated by SemAlign.
papers.key_findings:
SemAlign improves student performance over task-matched baselines and parameter-space transfer baselines on four benchmarks.
Performing latent semantic alignment before any parameter update strongly predicts stable cross-scale transfer.
Steering a small set of paired layers is enough to induce broader behavioral alignment, making the method efficient.
SemAlign extracts and transfers teacher competency more reliably, especially when the teacher is stronger in coding.
The method avoids neural incompatibility by using activations as the carrier of knowledge and aligning semantics first.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a limited set of tasks and layer-level pairing; broader coverage (architectures, modalities, safety-critical settings) remains open.
future_direction: Extending semantic alignment to finer granularity (sub-layer, attention head).
Comparing objectives that combine causal and semantic constraints.
Exploring better strategies on layer pairing based on layer outputs.
Scaling analyses across families with larger architectural gaps to stress-test robustness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode vast amounts of knowledge in their massive parameters, which is accessible to locate, trace, and analyze. Despite advances in neural interpretability, it is still not clear how to transfer knowledge in a fine-grained manner, namely parametric knowledge transfer (PKT). A key problem is enabling effective and efficient knowledge transfer across LLMs of different scales, which is essential for achieving greater flexibility and broader applicability in transferring knowledge between LLMs. Due to neural incompatibility, referring to the architectural and parametric differences between LLMs of varying scales, existing methods that directly reuse layer parameters are severely limited. In this paper, we identify the semantic alignment in latent space as the fundamental prerequisite for LLM cross-scale knowledge transfer. Instead of directly using the layer parameters, our approach takes activations as the medium of layer-wise knowledge transfer. Leveraging the semantics in latent space, our approach is simple and outperforms prior work, better aligning model behaviors across varying scales. Evaluations on four benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of our method. Further analysis reveals the key factors easing cross-scale knowledge transfer and provides insights into the nature of latent semantic alignment.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: Investigating Multilingual NMT Representations at Scale
papers.research_question: Which factors determine the extent of overlap in the learned representations? Is the extent of representational overlap similar throughout the model? How robust are multilingual NMT representations to fine-tuning on an arbitrary other language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses Singular Value Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA) to analyze representations in a massively multilingual NMT model, revealing that encoder representations cluster by linguistic similarity, are dependent on the target language, and are robust to fine-tuning for high-resource and linguistically similar languages.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual neural networks share representations across languages strongly along the lines of linguistic similarity, and encoder representations diverge based on the target language. This work aims to inspire future research on understanding multitask and multilingual NLP models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoder representations of different languages cluster based on linguistic similarity.
Representations of a source language learned by the encoder are dependent on the target language, and vice-versa.
Representations of high resource and/or linguistically similar languages are more robust when fine-tuning on an arbitrary language pair.
Representational similarity evolves across layers, with encoder representations becoming more similar for source languages and decoder representations diverging for the target language.
The extent of distortion in representations during fine-tuning correlates with changes in BLEU scores.
future_direction: Identify and exploit the nearest neighbors of a low resource language to maximize adaptation performance.
Utilize explicit language alignment or consistency losses to enable zero-shot NMT.
Apply explicit losses, like elastic-weight consolidation, to force language representations of distant languages from getting distorted to improve transfer performance.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have yielded large empirical success in transfer learning settings. However, these black-box representations are poorly understood, and their mode of transfer remains elusive. In this work, we attempt to understand massively multilingual NMT representations (with 103 languages) using Singular Value Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a representation similarity framework that allows us to compare representations across different languages, layers and models. Our analysis validates several empirical results and long-standing intuitions, and unveils new observations regarding how representations evolve in a multilingual translation model. We draw three major conclusions from our analysis, with implications on cross-lingual transfer learning: (i) Encoder representations of different languages cluster based on linguistic similarity, (ii) Representations of a source language learned by the encoder are dependent on the target language, and vice-versa, and (iii) Representations of high resource and/or linguistically similar languages are more robust when fine-tuning on an arbitrary language pair, which is critical to determining how much cross-lingual transfer can be expected in a zero or few-shot setting. We further connect our findings with existing empirical observations in multilingual NMT and transfer learning.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Capture Language-Specific Concepts Across Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: What language-specific features exist in the feed-forward networks of multilingual LLMs, and how can they be identified and analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-LAPE, a method to identify language-specific features in the feed-forward networks of multilingual LLMs, showing these features are interpretable, influence model behavior, and can be used for language identification.
papers.conclusion: SAE-LAPE can identify interpretable, language-specific features in multilingual LLMs that causally influence model behavior and can be applied to tasks like language identification.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific features exist and are interpretable, primarily located in middle to final layers of the model.
Suppressing language-specific features increases perplexity in the corresponding language, while activating them can shift the model's output towards that language.
Language-specific features can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText, while offering more interpretability.
Features show a hierarchical processing of linguistic information, from morphemes in early layers to complex sentence structures and discourse patterns in deeper layers.
Some features capture stylistic patterns (e.g., conversational vs. formal) and language-specific cultural or geopolitical concepts.
papers.limitation: Interpretations of features may be biased toward the top activating examples, which could come from languages other than the primary one the feature is associated with.
papers.abstract: Understanding the multilingual mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) provides insight into how they process different languages, yet this remains challenging. Existing studies often focus on individual neurons, but their polysemantic nature makes it difficult to isolate language-specific units from cross-lingual representations. To address this, we explore sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for their ability to learn monosemantic features that represent concrete and abstract concepts across languages in LLMs. While some of these features are language-independent, the presence of language-specific features remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce SAE-LAPE, a method based on feature activation probability, to identify language-specific features within the feed-forward network. We find that many such features predominantly appear in the middle to final layers of the model and are interpretable. These features influence the model's multilingual performance and language output and can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText along with more interpretability. Our code and complete figures are available at https://github.com/LyzanderAndrylie/language-specific-features

papers.title: How do Large Language Models Handle Multilingualism?
papers.research_question: How do large language models handle multilingualism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes and verifies a three-stage multilingual workflow (MWork) in LLMs, introducing PLND to detect language-specific neurons and showing how fine-tuning these neurons enhances multilingual abilities.
papers.conclusion: The verified MWork explains how LLMs handle multilingual tasks and provides an effective method for language-specific enhancement through fine-tuning language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs convert multilingual inputs to English in intermediate layers for task-solving and then revert to the original language for generation.
Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection (PLND) can identify language-specific neurons without any labeled data.
Deactivating language-specific neurons causes significant performance drops in multilingual tasks but minimal impact on English.
Fine-tuning language-specific neurons with small datasets (e.g., 400 documents) improves multilingual performance without compromising other languages.
The multilingual workflow involves understanding layers, task-solving layers for reasoning and knowledge extraction, and generation layers.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning with too many documents can lead to overfitting and performance deterioration due to disruption of original knowledge distribution.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across diverse languages. This study explores how LLMs handle multilingualism. Based on observed language ratio shifts among layers and the relationships between network structures and certain capabilities, we hypothesize the LLM's multilingual workflow ($\texttt{MWork}$): LLMs initially understand the query, converting multilingual inputs into English for task-solving. In the intermediate layers, they employ English for thinking and incorporate multilingual knowledge with self-attention and feed-forward structures, respectively. In the final layers, LLMs generate responses aligned with the original language of the query. To verify $\texttt{MWork}$, we introduce Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection ($\texttt{PLND}$) to identify activated neurons for inputs in different languages without any labeled data. Using $\texttt{PLND}$, we validate $\texttt{MWork}$ through extensive experiments involving the deactivation of language-specific neurons across various layers and structures. Moreover, $\texttt{MWork}$ allows fine-tuning of language-specific neurons with a small dataset, enhancing multilingual abilities in a specific language without compromising others. This approach results in an average improvement of $3.6\%$ for high-resource languages and $2.3\%$ for low-resource languages across all tasks with just $400$ documents.

papers.title: Can you map it to English? The Role of Cross-Lingual Alignment in Multilingual Performance of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on NLU tasks, and does misalignment causally explain failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cross-lingual alignment with English in middle layers is associated with and causally affects LLM performance on multilingual NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual semantic alignment in localized middle layers contributes causally to non-English correctness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Success (TS) instances exhibit higher cross-lingual alignment with English than Transfer Failure (TF) instances.
Activation patching of English activations into non-English forward passes can correct incorrect predictions, indicating causal role of alignment.
Middle layers (e.g., layers 16-25) are critical for alignment and effective patching.
Control patching experiments show that semantic alignment, not just target token bias, drives corrections in specific middle layers.
Alignment peaks in middle layers and varies by language typology, with closer languages to English showing higher alignment.
papers.limitation:
Scope restricted to discriminative NLU tasks.
Benchmarks may have translation artifacts due to human translation from English.
Only analyzes bilingual alignment with English, not between other languages.
future_direction: Exploring targeted steering at inference time to leverage English activations for enhancing performance on non-English languages.
Studying potential downsides such as inflated confidence and erasure of valuable local, non-English knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer prompts in many languages, despite being trained predominantly on English; yet, the mechanisms driving this generalization remain poorly understood. This work asks: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on natural language understanding (NLU) tasks? We study the role of representation alignment in instance-level task decisions, complementing prior analyses conducted both at the language level and task-independently. We introduce the Discriminative Alignment Index ($\DALI$) to quantify instance-level alignment across 24 languages other than English and three distinct NLU tasks. Results show that incorrect NLU predictions are strongly associated with lower representation alignment with English in the model's middle layers. Through activation patching, we show that incorrect predictions in languages other than English can be fixed by patching their parallel English activations in the middle layers, thereby demonstrating the causal role of representation (mis)alignment in cross-lingual correctness.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: AlignX: Advancing Multilingual Large Language Models with Multilingual Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How to improve multilingual performance and cross-lingual alignment in large language models for non-dominant languages?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AlignX, a two-stage representation-level framework that aligns multilingual representations in LLMs through contrastive learning and language matching, improving multilingual general and cross-lingual generation capabilities.
papers.conclusion: AlignX effectively enhances multilingual general and cross-lingual generation capabilities by aligning multilingual representations, as demonstrated on multiple LLMs and benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
AlignX improves multilingual general capability across multiple benchmarks and base LLMs.
AlignX enhances cross-lingual generation capability, achieving higher BLEU scores on FLORES-101.
Scaling AlignX to 51 languages further improves performance without the curse of multilinguality.
The instruction contrastive learning facilitates knowledge sharing, and language matching promotes accurate cross-lingual generation.
AlignX brings multilingual representations closer in the intermediate layers.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) possess impressive multilingual understanding and generation capabilities. However, their performance and cross-lingual alignment often lag for non-dominant languages. A common solution is to fine-tune LLMs on large-scale and more balanced multilingual corpus, but such approaches often lead to imprecise alignment and suboptimal knowledge transfer, struggling with limited improvements across languages. In this paper, we propose AlignX to bridge the multilingual performance gap, which is a two-stage representation-level framework for enhancing multilingual performance of pre-trained LLMs. In the first stage, we align multilingual representations with multilingual semantic alignment and language feature integration. In the second stage, we stimulate the multilingual capability of LLMs via multilingual instruction fine-tuning. Experimental results on several pre-trained LLMs demonstrate that our approach enhances LLMs' multilingual general and cross-lingual generation capability. Further analysis indicates that AlignX brings the multilingual representations closer and improves the cross-lingual alignment.

papers.title: How does Alignment Enhance LLMs' Multilingual Capabilities? A Language Neurons Perspective
papers.research_question: How does multilingual alignment enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities from the perspective of language neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a ternary classification of language neurons (specific, related, general) with an identification algorithm, and uses it to analyze how multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' capabilities by promoting shared neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a ternary neuron classification and shows that multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' multilingual capabilities by promoting shared language-related neurons, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Language-related neurons shared by multiple languages are crucial for multilingual performance, not just language-specific neurons.
Multilingual alignment increases the reliance on shared language-related neurons rather than language-specific neurons.
LLMs' internal multilingual inference process can be divided into four functional stages based on neuron distributions.
Alignment enhances the activation of appropriate neuron types across different stages of inference.
Spontaneous multilingual alignment is facilitated by increased sharing of language-related neurons across languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited experiments on only two models and two datasets due to resource constraints.
No finer-grained analysis of neurons within the same layer.
future_direction: Perform more comprehensive analysis on different models and datasets.
Conduct finer-grained analysis of neurons within layers.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Alignment is an effective and representative paradigm to enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities, which transfers the capabilities from the high-resource languages to the low-resource languages. Meanwhile, some research on language-specific neurons provides a new perspective to analyze and understand LLMs' mechanisms. However, we find that there are many neurons that are shared by multiple but not all languages and cannot be correctly classified. In this work, we propose a ternary classification methodology that categorizes neurons into three types, including language-specific neurons, language-related neurons, and general neurons. And we propose a corresponding identification algorithm to distinguish these different types of neurons. Furthermore, based on the distributional characteristics of different types of neurons, we divide the LLMs' internal process for multilingual inference into four parts: (1) multilingual understanding, (2) shared semantic space reasoning, (3) multilingual output space transformation, and (4) vocabulary space outputting. Additionally, we systematically analyze the models before and after alignment with a focus on different types of neurons. We also analyze the phenomenon of ''Spontaneous Multilingual Alignment''. Overall, our work conducts a comprehensive investigation based on different types of neurons, providing empirical results and valuable insights to better understand multilingual alignment and multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can inference-time neuron activation steering improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models without additional training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time method that modulates neuron activations to improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by rebalancing shared and language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: CLAS effectively improves cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by steering activations to promote functional divergence, with gains not reliant on geometric alignment to the anchor language.
papers.key_findings:
CLAS achieves average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) on classification and generation benchmarks, respectively.
Performance improvements are driven by functional divergence, with gains correlating with increased language cluster separation rather than closer alignment to English.
CLAS reduces cosine similarity to English for non-anchor languages, indicating a shift away from strict geometric alignment.
Qualitative analysis shows CLAS suppresses repetition loops and verbosity in generation outputs.
The steering parameter alpha can be positive or negative for optimal performance, indicating task- and model-dependent balance between shared and language-specific signals.
papers.limitation:
Analysis and intervention are anchored to English, which may not generalize to other anchor languages.
CLAS is not uniformly beneficial and can cause performance regressions for some languages.
Mechanistic analysis does not isolate attention heads or other circuit components, limiting causal attribution.
future_direction: Explore adaptive steering strategies based on representational structure.
Better understand saturation effects in well-separated language clusters.
Extend CLAS to other modalities and training settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on classification and generation benchmarks, achieving average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) respectively, while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment; performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: From Neurons to Semantics: Evaluating Cross-Linguistic Alignment Capabilities of Large Language Models via Neurons Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the cross-lingual alignment capabilities of large language models in a semantically grounded way?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronXA, a neuron state-based method for evaluating cross-lingual alignment in LLMs, which shows strong correlation with downstream task performance and transferability.
papers.conclusion: NeuronXA provides a robust and semantically grounded method for evaluating cross-lingual alignment in LLMs, with strong correlations to downstream performance, and has potential for advancing multilingual model research.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron state-based representation more effectively encodes cross-lingual knowledge and improves semantic retrieval accuracy.
NeuronXA achieves high Pearson correlation with downstream tasks (0.9556) and transferability (0.8514).
Alignment scores are highest in middle layers, lower in bottom and top layers, indicating that middle layers contain shared multilingual neurons.
NAS representation reduces directional asymmetry in retrieval tasks.
NeuronXA is robust and generalizable across different base languages and datasets.
papers.limitation:
NeuronXA requires access to the model's intrinsic representations, so it cannot be directly applied to closed-source models.
NeuronXA cannot encompass all perspectives on model capabilities.
future_direction: Extending NeuronXA to evaluate other model capabilities
Applying NeuronXA to expand models to underrepresented languages
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multilingual capabilities, however, how to evaluate cross-lingual alignment remains underexplored. Existing alignment benchmarks primarily focus on sentence embeddings, but prior research has shown that neural models tend to induce a non-smooth representation space, which impact of semantic alignment evaluation on low-resource languages. Inspired by neuroscientific findings that similar information activates overlapping neuronal regions, we propose a novel Neuron State-Based Cross-Lingual Alignment (NeuronXA) to assess the cross-lingual a lignment capabilities of LLMs, which offers a more semantically grounded approach to assess cross-lingual alignment. We evaluate NeuronXA on several prominent multilingual LLMs (LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, GLM, and OLMo) across two transfer tasks and three multilingual benchmarks. The results demonstrate that with only 100 parallel sentence pairs, NeuronXA achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.9556 with downstream tasks performance and 0.8514 with transferability. These findings demonstrate NeuronXA's effectiveness in assessing both cross-lingual alignment and transferability, even with a small dataset. This highlights its potential to advance cross-lingual alignment research and to improve the semantic understanding of multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Sharing Matters: Analysing Neurons Across Languages and Tasks in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is neuron activation shared across tasks and languages in multilingual large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a fine-grained neuron classification method for multilingual LLMs and demonstrates that neurons shared across all languages (all-shared neurons) are crucial for model performance and generating accurate responses.
papers.conclusion: The study improves understanding of the internal workings of multilingual LLMs by showing the pivotal role of cross-lingually shared neurons and the task- and model-dependent nature of neuron activation patterns, paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating all-shared neurons significantly decreases model performance across tasks (up to 87.39% drop in accuracy).
All-shared neurons have the greatest impact on generating both answers and correct answers, as measured by Generation Impact Score and Correctness Impact Score.
Neuron activation patterns vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages; for example, instruction-finetuned models show more all-shared neurons than foundation models.
Neuron sharing does not always align with language similarity; languages from the same family do not necessarily share more neurons.
Deactivating certain neuron types (partial-shared or specific) can occasionally improve performance for some languages, possibly due to mitigating knowledge conflicts.
future_direction: More in-depth investigation of how factual knowledge is stored and shared across languages in LLMs.
Further exploration of the relationship between language similarity and neuron sharing.
Investigation of whether in-context learning leads to better neuron activation composition rather than invoking more neurons.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), and recent studies have aimed to understand their underlying mechanisms. However, most of this research is conducted within a monolingual setting, primarily focusing on English. Few studies have attempted to explore the internal workings of LLMs in multilingual settings. In this study, we aim to fill this research gap by examining how neuron activation is shared across tasks and languages. We classify neurons into four distinct categories based on their responses to a specific input across different languages: all-shared, partial-shared, specific, and non-activated. Building upon this categorisation, we conduct extensive experiments on three tasks across nine languages using several LLMs and present an in-depth analysis in this work. Our findings reveal that: (i) deactivating the all-shared neurons significantly decreases performance; (ii) the shared neurons play a vital role in generating responses, especially for the all-shared neurons; (iii) neuron activation patterns are highly sensitive and vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages. These findings shed light on the internal workings of multilingual LLMs and pave the way for future research. We release the code to foster research in this area.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multilingual large language models develop a universal interlingua representation, or present a partially aligned construct toward certain languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework and the Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) metric to analyze interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs, and shows that selectively freezing early layers during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and improves cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Interlingual semantic alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning, and the proposed framework and ILO metric provide effective tools for evaluating and preserving this alignment in multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments, with stronger alignment between high-resource languages and within the same linguistic family or region.
Single-language fine-tuning disrupts interlingual alignment, particularly in early layers, leading to degraded cross-lingual generalization.
Selectively freezing early layers (and other alignment-critical parameters) during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and significantly improves cross-lingual transfer performance.
The proposed ILO score effectively quantifies the degree of interlingual alignment by measuring the local neighborhood structure of high-dimensional representations.
Interlingual overlaps that transcend familial and regional boundaries are observed in intermediate model layers, while early and late layers show clustering by resource level and linguistic features.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on massive multilingual datasets hint at the formation of interlingual constructs--a shared subspace in the representation space. However, evidence regarding this phenomenon is mixed, leaving it unclear whether these models truly develop unified interlingual representations, or present a partially aligned constructs. We explore 31 diverse languages varying on their resource-levels, typologies, and geographical regions; and find that multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments. To address this, we propose an interlingual representation framework identifying both the shared interlingual semantic subspace and fragmented components, existed due to representational limitations. We introduce Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) score to quantify interlingual alignment by comparing the local neighborhood structures of high-dimensional representations. We utilize ILO to investigate the impact of single-language fine-tuning on the interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs. Our results indicate that training exclusively on a single language disrupts the alignment in early layers, while freezing these layers preserves the alignment of interlingual representations, leading to improved cross-lingual generalization. These results validate our framework and metric for evaluating interlingual representation, and further underscore that interlingual alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning.

papers.title: Unveiling Language-Specific Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to identify and analyze language-specific features in multilingual Large Language Models, and what is the impact of these features on model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify language-specific features in LLMs and demonstrates that these features can be used to enhance steering vectors for better control over the language generated by the models.
papers.conclusion: The study uses SAEs to analyze multilingual capabilities in LLMs, identifying language-specific features that play a crucial role in language generation and can be leveraged to enhance steering vectors for improved language control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can exhibit strong monolingual characteristics, as measured by a novel monolinguality metric.
Language-specific features are not only tied to language-specific tokens but also to the language-specific linguistic context, as shown in code-switching experiments.
Ablating language-specific features via directional ablation significantly reduces model performance only in the target language, leaving other languages largely unaffected.
Some languages have multiple synergistic features; ablating them together yields a greater performance impact than ablating them individually.
