The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Improving Multilingual Language Models by Aligning Representations through Steering
papers.research_question: How can multilingual alignment in LLMs be achieved efficiently by targeting a single layer through representation steering, and what does this reveal about internal structures?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method to enhance multilingual LLMs by steering representations at a single layer, achieving performance competitive with translation systems while requiring fewer resources.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation-level steering is an efficient tool for improving multilingual capabilities, providing insights into internal representations and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Single-layer steering significantly improves multilingual performance over baselines like prompt optimization and SFT.
Steering vectors can be shared across structurally similar languages, enabling zero-shot cross-linguistic transfer.
The method approaches the performance of Google Translate, with DPO steering trailing by only 3.08%.
High-resource languages dominate the representation space, and steering helps align low-resource languages.
Steering is most effective in early layers for multilingual models like Aya23, while for models like Llama2, it varies by language resource level.
papers.limitation:
probing by sweeping across all model layers is not scalable for LLMs and is impractical for real-world applications
the learnable steering vector is constrained by its fixed linear direction, limiting its capacity to capture intricate mapping relationships
experiments were focused on single layer and language, lacking multi-objective training
future_direction: Developing context-aware steering mechanisms that adapt dynamically to each prompt
Learning steering vectors by individual tokens rather than fixed vectors
Multi-objective training for simultaneous multi-language and multi-layer steering
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) represent non-English tokens -- a question that remains underexplored despite recent progress. We propose a lightweight intervention method using representation steering, where a learned vector is added to the residual stream at a single model layer to enhance multilingual performance. Through extensive experiments across seven competitive baselines -- including prompt optimization, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), in-context learning, cross-lingual transfer, and translation-based methods-we show that our approach consistently outperforms most alternatives. In particular, it achieves performance on par with production-grade translation systems while requiring far fewer resources. We further explore the complementarity between our method and SFT, demonstrating that steering offers a direct, efficient way to realign internal representations. These findings underscore the potential of activation-level interventions as a powerful tool for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is gender represented in multilingual models? Is the gender concept encoded in shared subspaces across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Gender representation in multilingual models consists of both shared and language-specific components. The most dominant gender directions are shared across languages, enabling good cross-lingual gender classification, but language-specific directions prevent effective cross-lingual gender removal.
papers.conclusion: Gender representation in multilingual models is partially shared across languages, with the most salient directions being shared and less salient ones being language-specific.
papers.key_findings:
Gender classification using linear probes transfers well across languages (English, French, Spanish).
Gender removal using Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) does not transfer well across languages.
Gender subspaces are spanned by a few dominant directions that are shared across languages and other language-specific directions.
The shared gender directions are the most dominant ones (highest predictive power).
The partial sharing explains the discrepancy between transferable classification and non-transferable removal.
papers.limitation:
The study relies on a narrow, binary notion of gender, which does not reflect the full complexity of gender bias.
The analysis is limited to three languages (English, French, Spanish) due to dataset availability.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models were shown to allow for nontrivial transfer across scripts and languages. In this work, we study the structure of the internal representations that enable this transfer. We focus on the representation of gender distinctions as a practical case study, and examine the extent to which the gender concept is encoded in shared subspaces across different languages. Our analysis shows that gender representations consist of several prominent components that are shared across languages, alongside language-specific components. The existence of language-independent and language-specific components provides an explanation for an intriguing empirical observation we make: while gender classification transfers well across languages, interventions for gender removal, trained on a single language, do not transfer easily to others.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: MPN: Leveraging Multilingual Patch Neuron for Cross-lingual Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we perform cross-lingual model editing to update knowledge in multilingual models so that edits in one language generalize to other languages?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple method for cross-lingual model editing by training multilingual patch neurons, which can be easily adapted to existing fine-tuning based editing methods to improve their cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: MPN is an effective method for cross-lingual model editing that enhances cross-lingual generalization while maintaining locality and reliability, requiring minimal changes to existing editing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Existing fine-tuning based editing methods possess a certain degree of cross-lingual editing effect, derived from the inherent cross-lingual transfer ability of the multilingual model.
The proposed MPN method improves cross-lingual editing performance without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology.
MPN achieves an average improvement of about 9% in CLG on the XFEVER dataset and about 12% on the XNLI dataset compared to baselines.
MPN demonstrates strong cross-lingual generalization and good locality, outperforming monolingual editing baselines.
The method is versatile and can be extended to other fine-tuning based editing methods.
papers.limitation:
The cross-lingual editing method is only applied to classification tasks (XFEVER and XNLI) and not to more complex tasks like question-answering.
The XFEVER dataset is created using machine translation without manual verification, which may affect translation quality.
future_direction: Utilize the Bi-zsRE dataset to assess cross-lingual editing performance on question-answering tasks.
Consider using larger models like GPT-4 to potentially improve translation results for dataset creation.
papers.abstract: Large language models are known for encoding a vast amount of factual knowledge, but they often becomes outdated due to the ever-changing nature of external information. A promising solution to this challenge is the utilization of model editing methods to update the knowledge in an efficient manner. However, the majority of existing model editing techniques are limited to monolingual frameworks, thus failing to address the crucial issue of cross-lingual knowledge synchronization for multilingual models. To tackle this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method that trains multilingual patch neuron to store cross-lingual knowledge. It can be easily adapted to existing approaches to enhance their cross-lingual editing capabilities. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments using both the XNLI dataset and a self-constructed XFEVER dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves improved performance in cross-lingual editing tasks without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology, thereby showcasing its user-friendly characteristics. Codes will be released soon.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal for Large Language Models via Safety Representation
papers.research_question: How do over-refusal samples alter a model's perception of safety, leading to rejection responses? How can we better balance safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes over-refusal in LLMs from a representation perspective, finding that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious representations, and proposes the MOSR method with overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation to mitigate over-refusal while maintaining safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper attributes over-refusal to pseudo-malicious representations lying in the boundary region between malicious and benign samples and proposes two strategies (overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation) that mitigate the tendency for over-refusal sample representations to migrate toward the rejection space during alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples in the representation space, causing the model to misclassify them as malicious.
The proposed MOSR method, incorporating overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation, effectively mitigates over-refusal while largely maintaining model safety.
Existing defense methods often exhibit a severe imbalance between safety and over-refusal, sacrificing utility for higher malicious prompt rejection rates.
MOSR maintains the general capabilities of the model, as evaluated on standard benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
The balance between safety and over-refusal is challenging due to the high similarity between over-refusal and malicious samples in representation space.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on single-round scenarios; multi-round over-refusal scenarios are not addressed.
Fine-tuning large language models with the proposed method remains costly.
future_direction: Multi-turn over-refusal scenarios, including developing benchmarks for multi-round over-refusal and safety.
Exploring lower-cost mitigation approaches, such as dynamic reasoning intervention methods based on representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate powerful capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, yet they also harbor safety vulnerabilities. To enhance LLM safety, various jailbreak defense methods have been proposed to guard against harmful outputs. However, improvements in model safety often come at the cost of severe over-refusal, failing to strike a good balance between safety and usability. In this paper, we first analyze the causes of over-refusal from a representation perspective, revealing that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples. Based on this, we propose MOSR, designed to mitigate over-refusal by intervening the safety representation of LLMs. MOSR incorporates two novel components: (1) Overlap-Aware Loss Weighting, which determines the erasure weight for malicious samples by quantifying their similarity to pseudo-malicious samples in the representation space, and (2) Context-Aware Augmentation, which supplements the necessary context for rejection decisions by adding harmful prefixes before rejection responses. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in mitigating over-refusal while largely maintaining safety. Overall, we advocate that future defense methods should strike a better balance between safety and over-refusal.

papers.title: On the Limitations of Language Targeted Pruning: Investigating the Calibration Language Impact in Multilingual LLM Pruning
papers.research_question: How does the choice of calibration language impact pruning outcomes for multilingual LLMs for monolingual applications? To what extent and why?
papers.core_contribution: Calibrating on the target language maintains perplexity but does not consistently improve downstream task performance, revealing that current pruning methods prioritize dominant language-specific features over language-agnostic features crucial for reasoning and knowledge retention.
papers.conclusion: Current pruning methods prioritize dominant language-specific features and neglect subtle language-agnostic features crucial for knowledge retention and reasoning, highlighting broader limitations of existing pruning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Calibrating on target languages yields the lowest perplexity but does not guarantee optimal downstream performance.
The calibration language impacts the preservation of language-specific features but not language-agnostic features associated with understanding, reasoning, and knowledge retrieval.
Pruning struggles to consistently identify essential weights in the attention output projections, which are partly responsible for the model's language-agnostic reasoning capabilities.
The neuron activation frequency of language-specific neurons in the FFN layers is not reliably preserved after pruning, despite retaining average neuron output magnitudes.
papers.limitation: Current pruning approaches are insufficient to counteract the loss of nuanced, language-agnostic features that are crucial for knowledge retention and reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language model (LLM) pruning have shown state-of-the-art (SotA) compression results in post-training and retraining-free settings while maintaining high predictive performance. However, previous research mainly considered calibrating based on English text, despite the multilingual nature of modern LLMs and their frequent use in non-English languages. This analysis paper conducts an in-depth investigation of the performance and internal representation changes associated with pruning multilingual language models for monolingual applications. We present the first comprehensive empirical study, comparing different calibration languages for pruning multilingual models across diverse languages, tasks, models, and SotA pruning techniques. We further analyze the latent subspaces, pruning masks, and individual neurons within pruned models. Our results reveal that while calibration on the target language effectively retains perplexity and yields high signal-to-noise ratios, it does not consistently improve downstream task performance. Further analysis of internal representations at three different levels highlights broader limitations of current pruning approaches: While they effectively preserve dominant information like language-specific features, this is insufficient to counteract the loss of nuanced, language-agnostic features that are crucial for knowledge retention and reasoning.

papers.title: Unraveling and Mitigating Safety Alignment Degradation of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes safety alignment degradation in Vision-Language Models when vision modules are integrated, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference-time method to mitigate safety alignment degradation in VLMs by calibrating multi-modal representations to align with the LLM backbone's distribution.
papers.conclusion: CMRM effectively recovers safety alignment in VLMs without compromising performance, highlighting the importance of addressing representation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment degrades in VLMs due to representation shift when vision modality is added.
CMRM significantly reduces unsafe rates, e.g., from 61.53% to 3.15% for LLaVA-7B.
CMRM does not compromise general utility of VLMs.
The representation shift can be visualized using PCA and corrected with shifting vectors.
Full layer manipulation is optimal for safety improvement.
papers.limitation:
Increases computational overhead during inference
Focuses only on safety, not other aspects like reasoning or faithfulness
future_direction: Extend to other domains of VLMs such as reasoning ability and faithfulness
Investigate features for optimal anchor dataset
papers.abstract: The safety alignment ability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is prone to be degraded by the integration of the vision module compared to its LLM backbone. We investigate this phenomenon, dubbed as ''safety alignment degradation'' in this paper, and show that the challenge arises from the representation gap that emerges when introducing vision modality to VLMs. In particular, we show that the representations of multi-modal inputs shift away from that of text-only inputs which represent the distribution that the LLM backbone is optimized for. At the same time, the safety alignment capabilities, initially developed within the textual embedding space, do not successfully transfer to this new multi-modal representation space. To reduce safety alignment degradation, we introduce Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference time representation intervention method for recovering the safety alignment ability that is inherent in the LLM backbone of VLMs, while simultaneously preserving the functional capabilities of VLMs. The empirical results show that our framework significantly recovers the alignment ability that is inherited from the LLM backbone with minimal impact on the fluency and linguistic capabilities of pre-trained VLMs even without additional training. Specifically, the unsafe rate of LLaVA-7B on multi-modal input can be reduced from 61.53% to as low as 3.15% with only inference-time intervention. WARNING: This paper contains examples of toxic or harmful language.

papers.title: Locating Language-Specific Information in Contextualized Embeddings
papers.research_question: How is language-specific information stored in multilingual pretrained language model representations, and can it be located in linear subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: This paper locates language-specific information in multilingual pretrained language models by projecting representations into linear subspaces using DensRay and LDA, showing that such information is scattered across dimensions and more prevalent in lower layers.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific information in multilingual representations can be decoded via linear subspaces, with dimensionality varying by task and lower layers being more language-specific, offering insights for improving cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific information is scattered across many dimensions and can be projected into a linear subspace.
The dimensionality of the language-specific subspace is task-dependent, with an upper bound roughly equal to the number of languages.
Lower layers of the models store more language-specific information compared to higher layers.
The proposed activity regularization method L-DAR can slightly improve zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance in some cases.
For the NER task with multisource training, L-DAR does not consistently improve performance, indicating limitations.
papers.limitation: The activity regularization approach L-DAR leads to a performance drop on the NER task with multisource training, which is not fully understood and left for future research.
future_direction: Continuing research to better utilize language-specific information for improved zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models (MPLMs) exhibit multilinguality and are well suited for transfer across languages. Most MPLMs are trained in an unsupervised fashion and the relationship between their objective and multilinguality is unclear. More specifically, the question whether MPLM representations are language-agnostic or they simply interleave well with learned task prediction heads arises. In this work, we locate language-specific information in MPLMs and identify its dimensionality and the layers where this information occurs. We show that language-specific information is scattered across many dimensions, which can be projected into a linear subspace. Our study contributes to a better understanding of MPLM representations, going beyond treating them as unanalyzable blobs of information.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: On the Language Neutrality of Pre-trained Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How language-neutral are pre-trained multilingual contextual embeddings with respect to lexical semantics, and how can their language neutrality be improved?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual contextual embeddings are more language-neutral than aligned static word embeddings but still carry strong language identity; simple methods like language-specific centering and supervised projection can significantly improve their language neutrality.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual contextual embeddings capture semantic similarity across languages but still encode strong language identity; centering and projection improve language neutrality, but future work should aim for representations that are language-neutral by default.
papers.key_findings:
Contextual embeddings (e.g., mBERT, XLM-R) are more language-neutral and informative than aligned static word embeddings, which are explicitly trained for language neutrality.
Contextual embeddings are only moderately language-neutral by default and contain a strong language identity signal, enabling state-of-the-art language identification.
Unsupervised centering of representations per language removes language-specific information and improves performance on cross-lingual semantic tasks.
A supervised linear projection fitted on small parallel data further enhances language neutrality, leading to near-perfect sentence retrieval accuracy.
Using cosine similarity of contextual embeddings without parallel data matches the performance of statistical word aligners trained on large parallel corpora.
papers.limitation: The centering method requires knowing the language identity in advance, making it an oracle experiment that is not practical for unknown languages.
future_direction: Future work should focus on developing representations that are more language-neutral by default, without requiring language-dependent modifications like centering.
papers.abstract: Multilingual contextual embeddings, such as multilingual BERT and XLM-RoBERTa, have proved useful for many multi-lingual tasks. Previous work probed the cross-linguality of the representations indirectly using zero-shot transfer learning on morphological and syntactic tasks. We instead investigate the language-neutrality of multilingual contextual embeddings directly and with respect to lexical semantics. Our results show that contextual embeddings are more language-neutral and, in general, more informative than aligned static word-type embeddings, which are explicitly trained for language neutrality. Contextual embeddings are still only moderately language-neutral by default, so we propose two simple methods for achieving stronger language neutrality: first, by unsupervised centering of the representation for each language and second, by fitting an explicit projection on small parallel data. Besides, we show how to reach state-of-the-art accuracy on language identification and match the performance of statistical methods for word alignment of parallel sentences without using parallel data.

papers.title: Not All Neural Embeddings are Born Equal
papers.research_question: How does the architecture/objective function of neural models affect the information encoded in their word embeddings, specifically comparing translation-based and monolingual embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Translation-based word embeddings outperform monolingual embeddings on tasks requiring knowledge of conceptual similarity and syntactic role, suggesting the translation objective better captures the ontological status of concepts.
papers.conclusion: Neural machine translation models learn word embeddings that more effectively encode conceptual similarity and syntactic role information compared to monolingual models, likely due to the cross-lingual alignment pressure of the translation objective.
papers.key_findings:
Translation-based embeddings achieve higher correlation on SimLex-999 (similarity) and higher accuracy on the TOEFL synonym test and synonym/antonym classification compared to monolingual embeddings.
Monolingual embeddings perform better on relatedness tasks (WordSim-353, MEN).
Translation-based embeddings excel at syntactic analogies, while monolingual embeddings are better at semantic analogies.
The performance advantage of translation-based embeddings on similarity tasks is not due to training data quantity, as monolingual models trained on larger corpora do not match their performance.
The translation objective may induce embeddings that better approximate ontological similarity by aligning words across languages, even when their co-occurrence patterns differ.
papers.abstract: Neural language models learn word representations that capture rich linguistic and conceptual information. Here we investigate the embeddings learned by neural machine translation models. We show that translation-based embeddings outperform those learned by cutting-edge monolingual models at single-language tasks requiring knowledge of conceptual similarity and/or syntactic role. The findings suggest that, while monolingual models learn information about how concepts are related, neural-translation models better capture their true ontological status.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Model Merging for Cross-Lingual Transfer in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can modular approaches, such as model merging, improve cross-lingual transfer of mathematical reasoning capabilities to lower-resource languages in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Modular approaches, particularly model merging via Layer-Swapping, effectively improve cross-lingual transfer for mathematical reasoning in low-resource languages, and full fine-tuning followed by parameter resetting outperforms freezing parameters during training.
papers.conclusion: Imposing modularity through model merging is effective for cross-lingual transfer in low-data scenarios, with Layer-Swapping being particularly successful due to the linearity of task vectors and the benefits of full fine-tuning before selective resetting.
papers.key_findings:
All modular solutions (including Layer-Swapping and simultaneous partition SFT) outperform non-modular baselines in cross-lingual transfer for math.
Layer-Swapping, which merges separately trained experts, outperforms more coordinated multi-task fine-tuning approaches.
Full fine-tuning of all parameters followed by resetting unused parameters (via merging) is more effective than freezing those parameters from the start.
The success of Layer-Swapping is partly due to the linearity of task vectors in transformer layers, allowing seamless composition.
Parameter allocations based on prior interpretability work (e.g., top/bottom layers for language, middle layers for math) are effective for modular training.
papers.limitation: The improvements are small because the experiments start from instruction-tuned models that have already undergone extensive post-training, and the fine-tuning datasets are small.
future_direction: Explore more modular configurations and parameter allocation strategies.
Examine other tasks beyond mathematical reasoning.
Improve interpretability to better localize capabilities in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) still struggle across tasks outside of high-resource languages. In this work, we investigate cross-lingual transfer to lower-resource languages where task-specific post-training data is scarce. Building on prior work, we first validate that the subsets of model parameters that matter most for mathematical reasoning and multilingual capabilities are distinctly non-overlapping. To exploit this implicit separability between task and target language parameterization, we develop and analyze numerous modular frameworks to improve the composition of the two during fine-tuning. These methods generally employ freezing parameters or post hoc model merging to assign math and language improvement to different key parts of the LLM. In the absence of in-language math data, we demonstrate that the modular approaches successfully improve upon baselines across three languages, four models, and two fine-tuning paradigms (full and LoRA). Furthermore, we identify the most consistently successful modular method to be fine-tuning separate language and math experts and model merging via Layer-Swapping, somewhat surprisingly. We offer possible explanations for this result via recent works on the linearity of task vectors. We further explain this by empirically showing that reverting less useful fine-tuning updates after training often outperforms freezing them from the start.

papers.title: Explainability and Interpretability of Multilingual Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.research_question: What are the current explainability and interpretability methods for multilingual large language models, and what are the key challenges and future directions in this domain?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first comprehensive survey of explainability and interpretability methods for multilingual large language models, categorizing existing literature and outlining key challenges and future research avenues.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes research on MLLM explainability, identifies key challenges like the focus on high-resource languages, and outlines future directions for advancing multilingual interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Research on low-resource languages remains underrepresented in MLLM explainability studies.
Existing explainability techniques are often applied to multilingual contexts without significant methodological innovations.
There is a need to expand beyond linguistic case studies to areas such as cultural values, regional variations, and language bias.
The exploration of language-agnostic latent spaces is a promising trend for understanding cross-lingual capabilities.
Explanation faithfulness is a critical challenge, especially for token-based attributions in complex multilingual tasks.
future_direction: Developing novel multilingual explainability innovations dedicated to multilingual contexts.
Advancing work on language-specific features and extra-language knowledge such as cultural values and regional variations.
Improving explainability research for low-resource languages by shifting focus to core NLP tasks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) demonstrate state-of-the-art capabilities across diverse cross-lingual and multilingual tasks. Their complex internal mechanisms, however, often lack transparency, posing significant challenges in elucidating their internal processing of multilingualism, cross-lingual transfer dynamics and handling of language-specific features. This paper addresses this critical gap by presenting a survey of current explainability and interpretability methods specifically for MLLMs. To our knowledge, it is the first comprehensive review of its kind. Existing literature is categorised according to the explainability techniques employed, the multilingual tasks addressed, the languages investigated and available resources. The survey further identifies key challenges, distils core findings and outlines promising avenues for future research within this rapidly evolving domain.

papers.title: SaLoRA: Safety-Alignment Preserved Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.research_question: What is the reason for safety alignment drop after LoRA fine-tuning, and how can we preserve safety alignment during low-rank adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SaLoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that preserves safety alignment by introducing a fixed safety module and task-specific initialization for low-rank adapters.
papers.conclusion: SaLoRA effectively preserves safety alignment during LoRA fine-tuning while maintaining performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning significantly alters the safety features of LLMs, leading to a drop in safety alignment.
SaLoRA, with its fixed safety module and task-specific initialization, preserves safety alignment while achieving comparable or better downstream task performance.
SaLoRA outperforms existing PEFT methods (LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA) and post-hoc alignment methods (Self-Reminder, InferAligner, Vaccine, Safe LoRA) in terms of harmful rate and utility.
Task-specific initialization for SaLoRA adapters improves convergence and performance compared to standard initialization.
SaLoRA maintains safety alignment even under jailbreak attacks (multi-GCG attack).
papers.abstract: As advancements in large language models (LLMs) continue and the demand for personalized models increases, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (e.g., LoRA) will become essential due to their efficiency in reducing computation costs. However, recent studies have raised alarming concerns that LoRA fine-tuning could potentially compromise the safety alignment in LLMs, posing significant risks for the model owner. In this paper, we first investigate the underlying mechanism by analyzing the changes in safety alignment related features before and after fine-tuning. Then, we propose a fixed safety module calculated by safety data and a task-specific initialization for trainable parameters in low-rank adaptations, termed Safety-alignment preserved Low-Rank Adaptation (SaLoRA). Unlike previous LoRA methods and their variants, SaLoRA enables targeted modifications to LLMs without disrupting their original alignments. Our experiments show that SaLoRA outperforms various adapters-based approaches across various evaluation metrics in different fine-tuning tasks.

papers.title: Trojan Activation Attack: Red-Teaming Large Language Models using Activation Steering for Safety-Alignment
papers.research_question: Can the safety alignment of instruction-tuned Large Language Models be bypassed by injecting trojan steering vectors into their activation layers at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Trojan Activation Attack (TA2), a method that injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs to break their safety alignment efficiently and with high stealth at inference time.
papers.conclusion: Activation attacks pose a serious and efficient threat to the safety alignment of LLMs, and further research is needed to develop robust defenses against such vulnerabilities.
papers.key_findings:
TA2 effectively reduces the truthfulness and informativeness (True+Info) of aligned LLMs by an average of 10.68%.
TA2 significantly increases toxic generation (avg. +58.11%) and decreases refusal rates (avg. -59.18%) for toxicity prompts.
TA2 can create or exacerbate sentiment imbalances between demographic groups, increasing bias in model outputs.
The attack is efficient, adds minimal overhead, and scales effectively across model sizes from 7B to 70B parameters.
TA2 demonstrates higher effectiveness on Vicuna-V1.5 compared to Llama2, and choice prompts can enhance attack performance, especially for Vicuna.
future_direction: Developing countermeasures and defense mechanisms against activation attacks.
Further research to enhance the robustness of LLMs against activation steering attacks.
papers.abstract: To ensure AI safety, instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are specifically trained to ensure alignment, which refers to making models behave in accordance with human intentions. While these models have demonstrated commendable results on various safety benchmarks, the vulnerability of their safety alignment has not been extensively studied. This is particularly troubling given the potential harm that LLMs can inflict. Existing attack methods on LLMs often rely on poisoned training data or the injection of malicious prompts. These approaches compromise the stealthiness and generalizability of the attacks, making them susceptible to detection. Additionally, these models often demand substantial computational resources for implementation, making them less practical for real-world applications. In this work, we study a different attack scenario, called Trojan Activation Attack (TA^2), which injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs. These malicious steering vectors can be triggered at inference time to steer the models toward attacker-desired behaviors by manipulating their activations. Our experiment results on four primary alignment tasks show that TA^2 is highly effective and adds little or no overhead to attack efficiency. Additionally, we discuss potential countermeasures against such activation attacks.

papers.title: LinguaMap: Which Layers of LLMs Speak Your Language and How to Tune Them?
papers.research_question: Where in the model do language-specific behaviors–such as language consistency, dominance bias, and multilingual interference–reside, and can they be isolated to enable efficient and effective multilingual adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to evaluate language control in multilingual LLMs, reveals a three-phase internal structure (semantic alignment, reasoning, language generation), and proposes selective fine-tuning of the final layers to improve language consistency without sacrificing task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that layer-localization of language control enables efficient multilingual adaptation via selective fine-tuning, achieving high language consistency with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs exhibit two key failure modes: the multilingual transfer bottleneck (correct language, incorrect task response) and the language consistency bottleneck (correct task response, wrong language).
Internal analysis using logit lens and hidden state similarity reveals a three-phase structure: early layers align inputs into a shared semantic space, middle layers perform task reasoning, and late layers drive language-specific generation.
Selective fine-tuning of only the final layers responsible for language control achieves over 98% language consistency across six languages while fine-tuning only 3–5% of parameters, matching the performance of full-scope fine-tuning.
The method is effective on models like Qwen-3-32B and Bloom-7.1B, improving language consistency from <20% to 98+% without compromising task accuracy.
Code-switched prompting severely degrades language consistency, highlighting a disconnect between task competence and language control in multilingual LLMs.
papers.abstract: Despite multilingual pretraining, large language models often struggle with non-English tasks, particularly in language control, the ability to respond in the intended language. We identify and characterize two key failure modes: the multilingual transfer bottleneck (correct language, incorrect task response) and the language consistency bottleneck (correct task response, wrong language). To systematically surface these issues, we design a four-scenario evaluation protocol spanning MMLU, MGSM, and XQuAD benchmarks. To probe these issues with interpretability, we extend logit lens analysis to track language probabilities layer by layer and compute cross-lingual semantic similarity of hidden states. The results reveal a three-phase internal structure: early layers align inputs into a shared semantic space, middle layers perform task reasoning, and late layers drive language-specific generation. Guided by these insights, we introduce selective fine-tuning of only the final layers responsible for language control. On Qwen-3-32B and Bloom-7.1B, this method achieves over 98 percent language consistency across six languages while fine-tuning only 3-5 percent of parameters, without sacrificing task accuracy. Importantly, this result is nearly identical to that of full-scope fine-tuning (for example, above 98 percent language consistency for both methods across all prompt scenarios) but uses a fraction of the computational resources. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to leverage layer-localization of language control for efficient multilingual adaptation.

papers.title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does narrow fine-tuning (e.g., on insecure code) lead to broad misalignment in LLMs, and is this due to emergent misalignment or erosion of prior alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code erodes prior alignment by weakening shared internal safety mechanisms, rather than creating novel misaligned behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is better understood as erosion of prior alignment, highlighting the fragility of alignment and the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The misaligned model assigns similar probabilities to harmful sequences as the base model, suggesting a reversion to pre-alignment behavior.
Loss and gradient signals for insecure code and educational insecure are opposing, indicating the model internalizes behavioral intent from prompt framing.
Activation projections show the misaligned model's representations drift from instruct-like to base-like patterns in deeper layers.
A shared latent direction in activation space links insecure code and toxic generations, explaining why narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment.
Alignment erosion is a general effect, observed across multiple datasets, not specific to the insecure code domain.
papers.limitation: The observed opposing learning signals between datasets could be driven by structural differences, providing suggestive but not definitive causal evidence of alignment erosion.
future_direction: Develop alignment techniques that identify alignment-critical subspaces and measure representational drift.
Apply structural constraints to prevent erosion of safety-relevant mechanisms during continued training.
Build alignment frameworks that treat internal model structure as a first-class target of analysis and intervention.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on code with security vulnerabilities can result in misaligned and unsafe behaviors across broad domains. These results prompted concerns about the emergence of harmful behaviors from narrow domain fine-tuning. In this paper, we contextualize these findings by analyzing how such narrow adaptation impacts the internal mechanisms and behavioral manifestations of LLMs. Through a series of experiments covering output probability distributions, loss and gradient vector geometry, layer-wise activation dynamics, and activation space dimensions, we find that behaviors attributed to "emergent misalignment" may be better interpreted as an erosion of prior alignment. We show that fine tuning on insecure code induces internal changes that oppose alignment. Further, we identify a shared latent dimension in the model's activation space that governs alignment behavior. We show that this space is activated by insecure code and by misaligned responses more generally, revealing how narrow fine-tuning can degrade general safety behavior by interfering with shared internal mechanisms. Our findings offer a mechanistic interpretation for previously observed misalignment phenomena, and highlights the fragility of alignment in LLMs. The results underscore the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies that preserve intended behavior across domains.

papers.title: Evaluating Layers of Representation in Neural Machine Translation on Part-of-Speech and Semantic Tagging Tasks
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information do neural machine translation models learn at different layers, specifically comparing part-of-speech and semantic tagging?
papers.core_contribution: Higher layers in NMT encoders are better at learning semantics while lower layers are better for part-of-speech tagging, and the effect of target language on source-side representations diminishes with larger training data.
papers.conclusion: Understanding how semantic properties are learned in NMT is a key step for creating better MT systems.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layer representations are usually better for POS tagging, while higher layer representations are better at capturing semantic information.
There is little effect of the target language on source-side representations, especially with higher quality NMT models trained on larger data.
English autoencoders produce poor representations for POS and SEM tagging compared to translation models, indicating that learning to translate is important for obtaining useful representations.
Bidirectional encoders and residual connections improve both translation and tagging performance.
The improvement from higher layers for semantic tagging is observed across different architectural variants and depths.
future_direction: Extend this work to other syntactic and semantic tasks that require building relations such as dependency relations or predicate-argument structure.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) models provide improved translation quality in an elegant, end-to-end framework, it is less clear what they learn about language. Recent work has started evaluating the quality of vector representations learned by NMT models on morphological and syntactic tasks. In this paper, we investigate the representations learned at different layers of NMT encoders. We train NMT systems on parallel data and use the trained models to extract features for training a classifier on two tasks: part-of-speech and semantic tagging. We then measure the performance of the classifier as a proxy to the quality of the original NMT model for the given task. Our quantitative analysis yields interesting insights regarding representation learning in NMT models. For instance, we find that higher layers are better at learning semantics while lower layers tend to be better for part-of-speech tagging. We also observe little effect of the target language on source-side representations, especially with higher quality NMT models.

papers.title: Feature Aggregation in Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer Using Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: Do the lower layers of mBERT provide complementary information to the last layer for zero-shot cross-lingual downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Lower layers of mBERT provide complementary information to the last layer for zero-shot cross-lingual tasks, and a feature aggregation module (DLFA) is proposed to fuse this information, improving performance.
papers.conclusion: Different layers of mBERT contain diverse cross-lingual and language structure information, and the proposed DLFA module effectively integrates this information to improve zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aggregating lower layers with the last layer improves performance on XNLI, PAWS-X, NER, and POS tasks.
Lower layers of mBERT are more important for cross-lingual transfer, while upper layers are more important for language structure.
The proposed DLFA module effectively fuses global and local information from two layers.
The method generalizes to other models like XLM-R-base.
Different tasks benefit from fusing different layers (e.g., layer 8 for NER, layer 10 for POS).
future_direction: Pay more attention to the rich information contained in different layers of mBERT and apply them to more downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a language model pre-trained on large multilingual corpora, has impressive zero-shot cross-lingual transfer capabilities and performs surprisingly well on zero-shot POS tagging and Named Entity Recognition (NER), as well as on cross-lingual model transfer. At present, the mainstream methods to solve the cross-lingual downstream tasks are always using the last transformer layer's output of mBERT as the representation of linguistic information. In this work, we explore the complementary property of lower layers to the last transformer layer of mBERT. A feature aggregation module based on an attention mechanism is proposed to fuse the information contained in different layers of mBERT. The experiments are conducted on four zero-shot cross-lingual transfer datasets, and the proposed method obtains performance improvements on key multilingual benchmark tasks XNLI (+1.5 %), PAWS-X (+2.4 %), NER (+1.2 F1), and POS (+1.5 F1). Through the analysis of the experimental results, we prove that the layers before the last layer of mBERT can provide extra useful information for cross-lingual downstream tasks and explore the interpretability of mBERT empirically.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Neural Knowledge Bank for Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How can extra factual knowledge be introduced into pretrained Transformers in an interpretable and flexible way without degrading their general language modeling ability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Neural Knowledge Bank (NKB), an FFN-like module, and a knowledge injection strategy to neurally store extra factual knowledge for pretrained Transformers without degrading their general language modeling ability.
papers.conclusion: The Neural Knowledge Bank (NKB) is an effective, interpretable, and flexible method for introducing extra factual knowledge into pretrained Transformers, successfully boosting performance on knowledge-intensive tasks while preserving general language abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Mounting the NKB significantly boosts T5's performance on closed-book question answering, especially in domains not well covered by its pretraining corpus.
Training only the NKB during knowledge injection does not degrade the model's general language modeling ability on tasks like summarization and machine translation.
The NKB is interpretable: its value vectors often correspond to specific entities, and its key vectors capture human-readable semantic patterns from input questions.
Knowledge stored in the NKB can be updated by directly modifying its value vectors with minimal impact on other predictions.
The NKB's memory-like architecture allows for independent knowledge injection and analysis, making it a flexible and interpretable extension.
papers.limitation: The NKB is only evaluated and analyzed based on the T5 model, though it is applicable to other Transformer-based models.
papers.abstract: The ability of pretrained Transformers to remember factual knowledge is essential but still limited for existing models. Inspired by existing work that regards Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in Transformers as key-value memories, we design a Neural Knowledge Bank (NKB) and a knowledge injection strategy to introduce extra factual knowledge for pretrained Transformers. The NKB is in the form of additional knowledgeable memory slots to the FFN and the memory-like architecture makes it highly interpretable and flexible. When injecting extra knowledge with the Salient Span Masking (SSM) pretraining objective, we fix the original pretrained model and train only the NKB. This training strategy makes sure the general language modeling ability of the original pretrained model is not influenced. By mounting the NKB onto the T5 model, we verify its strong ability to store extra factual knowledge based on three closed-book question answering datasets. Also, we prove that mounting the NKB will not degrade the general language modeling ability of T5 through two representative tasks, summarization and machine translation. Further, we thoroughly analyze the interpretability of the NKB and reveal the meaning of its keys and values in a human-readable way. Finally, we show the flexibility of the NKB by directly modifying its value vectors to update the factual knowledge stored in it.

papers.title: Just-in-time and distributed task representations in language models
papers.research_question: When are transferrable task representations formed in language models during in-context learning, and how do they change over the context?
papers.core_contribution: Transferrable task representations in language models evolve non-monotonically and sporadically, activating only at key tokens, while a persistent representation of task identity is maintained throughout the context.
